One exchange. One café menu. One old screenshot. One charging port. One public selfie. Each was enough to lose money, privacy or your own face, and every one of them looked completely normal.

I ran every check twice, once with Grok and once with Claude Code. Same prompts, same results, so use whichever you already pay for. All you need is a laptop, sometimes a cable, and about ten minutes per case.
Each case goes story first, then how real it is, a prompt to paste, the manual version, and how to shut it down.

⠀
the ride felt off. the driver used her name before she told him. i opened my laptop and asked Grok to scan every wifi and bluetooth device around us.
⠀
→ wifi → 14 networks
→ bluetooth → 23 devices
→ open hotspot → 'IPC_7F3A' → a cheap shenzhen ip-camera module
→ one unnamed bluetooth device → -41 dBm → not a phone
⠀
we drove 2.1 km. the signal never changed. it was inside the car.
⠀
→ device 1 → dashboard vent → inside the air freshener
→ device 2 → rear headrest → 40 cm from my wife's head → microphone
→ camera angle → the back seat, at phone-screen height
→ not a Tesla part → aftermarket, plugged in by someone
⠀
the car had free wifi. my wife was connected to it. so was the camera.
⠀
→ upload every 30 seconds → 47.243.***.18 → Hong Kong
→ 1.8 MB per upload → video and audio
→ audio → speech-to-text → keyword filter
→ keywords → card, code, password, pin, address
→ live stream → 1 viewer online → right now
⠀
i stopped scrolling. the 1 didn't go away.
⠀
i asked Grok to trace the account it uploaded to.
⠀
→ account → fl33t_***
→ 212 cameras → all moving → all in cars
→ 14 cities → mostly airport routes after 10pm
→ 31,000 rides recorded in 7 months
→ every ride auto-tagged → bank, crypto, home address
⠀
then Grok found our ride. and the one before it.
⠀
→ tagged HIGH VALUE → 4 minutes ago
→ transcript → her bank call → card ending 4417 → "the code from the sms"
→ a second recording of her → same car → 19 days ago
→ drop-off point on that ride → our home address
⠀
that's how the driver knew her name.
⠀
→ next stop → a telegram channel
→ 9,400 buyers → $25 per high-value ride
→ 3 rides from this same car already sold today
⠀
what Grok did next:
⠀
→ saved 41 files of evidence → timestamps and gps track
→ blocked card 4417 → bank fraud team notified
→ 11 minutes later → someone tried to spend $3,800 on it → declined
→ filed a safety report with the ride app → driver and plate
→ drafted a police report → ip, account, channel, both recordings
⠀
the driver was suspended 6 minutes after the report. we got out at the next light and walked home the long way.
⠀
211 other cars on that account are still driving tonight. most of them are waiting at airports.
⠀
if you take taxis at night, open your laptop next time you get in. it takes 2 minutes.

hits.text:
this is absolutely unreal

Google open-sourced Harness², and it lets an agent rebuild its own harness on every new task

the harness is everything around the model: system prompt, guardrails, memory, tool guidance, subagents, skills, scripts, plugins

usually a person designs it once, and every task after that runs on the same fixed setup

Harness² edits that setup per task and never touches the model weights:
> propose - the agent writes edits to its own harness
> probe - it runs a few candidate versions on the same task
> compose - it builds a better harness from how those runs differed

the clever part: it learns from the differences between runs, so it works on tasks that have no answer key or grader

NVIDIA and MIT researchers used Karpathy's loop to cut agent harness costs in half, and put the whole method in a 15-page PDF

the shift: keep the same LLM and the same benchmark, change only the harness

how they built it:

step 1 -> read the agent's execution logs: repeated actions, growing context, oversized outputs. find where tokens stop moving the task forward

step 2 -> run Karpathy's loop on the harness: propose, implement, review, test, keep or discard. lock the quality and cost gates before the search starts

four fixes survived:

step 3 -> fuse actions: edit the file and run its planned test in one tool call, with no model round trip between them

step 4 -> compact at finished steps, only when the savings beat the cost of rewriting the cached context

step 5 -> stop replaying huge outputs: archive them, keep a handle and a short excerpt, pull exact pages when needed

step 6 -> hand log reading to a cheaper model, then check its evidence against the original. if the check fails, return the full log

how to steal it for your own agents:

step 7 -> start with one mechanism and measure it against your current setup before you stack all four

step 8 -> freeze the changes, then test on tasks it hasn't seen. track completion, API cost and tokens together, because a cheaper failure is still a failure

the result:
> 50-54% lower API costs than native Codex and Claude Code on EdgeBench, same main models
> against Pi: about a third cheaper, 45-49% fewer tokens, roughly 94% of its average score kept

the engineer who brings that chart to a planning meeting is the one who gets the agent budget

the reusable harness setup that gets Opus 5.5 through long tasks is below ↓

virals.text:
"Frontier LLMs barely add comments anymore." Codex: 1 comment line in 190. Claude Code: 74 in 317.

@icanvardar asked 45K people if they noticed. So we gave Claude Code (Opus 5.5) and Codex (GPT-6.1 Terra) the same real bug ticket 15 times each and counted every comment line they added.

→ Codex: 1 comment line in 190 added lines, none at all in 14 of 15 runs
→ Claude Code: 74 comment lines in 317, at least one in all 15 runs
→ Hidden checks passed: Codex 105 of 105, Claude Code 101 of 105

The twist: the repo itself had zero # comments. Codex matched it. Claude Code ignored it and wrote down why the bug happened: "truncating here discarded partial refills, so frequent polling never recovered."

So it is not frontier models. It is one of them, matching the repo it was given.

Do you keep your agent's comments, or strip them before review?

Repost this now, because every team reviews agent diffs and nobody counted the comments.

Follow @stas_sorokin_ for numbers from AI systems running in real production.

outsiders.text:
"Frontier LLMs barely add comments anymore." Codex: 1 comment line in 190. Claude Code: 74 in 317.

@icanvardar asked 45K people if they noticed. So we gave Claude Code (Opus 5.5) and Codex (GPT-6.1 Terra) the same real bug ticket 15 times each and counted every comment line they added.

→ Codex: 1 comment line in 190 added lines, none at all in 14 of 15 runs
→ Claude Code: 74 comment lines in 317, at least one in all 15 runs
→ Hidden checks passed: Codex 105 of 105, Claude Code 101 of 105

The twist: the repo itself had zero # comments. Codex matched it. Claude Code ignored it and wrote down why the bug happened: "truncating here discarded partial refills, so frequent polling never recovered."

So it is not frontier models. It is one of them, matching the repo it was given.

Do you keep your agent's comments, or strip them before review?

Repost this now, because every team reviews agent diffs and nobody counted the comments.

Follow @stas_sorokin_ for numbers from AI systems running in real production.
